listenings.text: Fabia, this is David. Here is the list from head office. Two things are not negotiable. There must be a full audit trail on every change. And if there is a breach, we must be notified within twenty-four hours, in writing. One more thing we recommend: there should be a quarterly call between your team and ours. And a warning: legal still has to review the contract. That may take two more weeks.

Fabia, this is David again. Let me tell you how I lost an account. They asked me who has access to the data. I said, only a few people, usually. They asked what happens if there is a leak. I said we would try to tell them quickly. They asked about their auditors. I said we could probably arrange something. Then they asked for the same answers in writing. After that, they stopped replying.

matching.title: Match the word to its meaning
defs: the record of who changed what, and when
legal responsibility if something goes wrong
the duty not to share what you know

items.situation: "Who can see our payroll data?" One sentence, with the number.
tips: Four people: three analysts and one partner.

items.situation: "What happens if there is a breach?" One sentence, with must.
tips: We must notify you within twenty-four hours, in writing.
That is not our policy, it is regulatory.

items.situation: You want their data by the tenth. One question, with could.
tips: Could you send us the data by the tenth?
We would need it by ... to be safe.

items.situation: They ask for read-only access for the auditors. One sentence, with can.
tips: Yes, we can give your auditors read-only access.
That is not required, but we can.

items.situation: At 400 employees onboarding takes a week longer. One sentence.
tips: The process is scalable, but onboarding may take an extra week.
Onboarding may take an extra week at that volume.
I'd rather tell you now than in month two.

arguebank.label: Useful language
items: B sounds ... , and on compliance that reads as risk.
A client wants to hear must, not we try to.
If I were the client, I would ...
That answer leaves too much open.
You can be firm and still be polite.
